query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, controlled thermal aging in high-temperature oxidizing and corrosive environments triggers the selective coarsening and phase transformation of metastable Mg-rich intermetallic phases. These changes create local compositional gradients that modify the nucleation and adherence of protective oxide scales during oxidation and alter localized corrosion behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, metastable microstructure with a fine dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallic phases embedded in solid solution phases, all within a density constraint below 6 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal aging together with high-temperature oxidizing (∼800–1200 °C) and accelerated corrosive exposures to samples sharing the identical as‐cast microstructure.
generation.conditions: A controlled-variable experiment comparing the as‐cast baseline against samples subjected to thermal aging under oxidizing and corrosive conditions. Testing is performed at temperatures representative of high-temperature oxidation and under aggressive corrosive media.
generation.structural_mediator: The selective coarsening and transformation (phase separation or redistribution) of Mg-rich intermetallic phases during thermal aging.
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging drives the metastable Mg-rich phases to coarsen and undergo phase transformations. This evolution changes local chemical gradients, which in turn influence the kinetics, morphology, and adherence of protective oxide scales during high-temperature oxidation and modify localized electrochemical behavior, impacting corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as‐cast baseline, the thermally aged samples will exhibit observable coarsening or redistribution of Mg-rich phases and display altered oxidation kinetics (such as more adherent or uniform oxide scales) along with changed (potentially improved) localized corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: As-cast alloy with a non-equilibrium microstructure containing finely dispersed Mg-rich intermetallics and solid solution phases.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to lightweight high-entropy alloys containing Mg designed to have densities below 6 g/cm³. It is specific to systems where constituent property differences lead to inherent phase complexity and is tested under defined high-temperature oxidation (800–1200 °C) and accelerated corrosion conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of the Mg-rich phase transformations and the magnitude of the resulting changes in oxidation and corrosion behavior remain uncertain. Additional experiments are needed to optimize thermal aging parameters and to fully map the microstructural evolution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples with identical as-cast microstructures. Subject one set to controlled thermal aging under high-temperature oxidizing and corrosive conditions while keeping the other set as an untreated baseline. Employ in situ XRD and TEM to track the evolution of Mg-rich intermetallic phases. Simultaneously, measure oxidation kinetics via mass change and scale characterization and evaluate corrosion resistance using electrochemical tests and localized attack analyses.
measurements: Microstructural phase evolution (coarsening or phase transformation of Mg-rich intermetallics via XRD/TEM)
Oxidation kinetics and oxide scale quality (mass change, morphology, adherence tests)
Corrosion resistance (electrochemical measurements, localized corrosion assessment)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not produce significant changes in the size, distribution, or phase constitution of Mg-rich intermetallics, or if no measurable differences in oxidation kinetics and corrosion resistance are observed between the heat-treated and as-cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The alloys JZ1 and JZ2 had lower Ge and Sn concentrations and the same but lower Ti concentrations than the alloys studied by Vellios and Tsakiropoulos (see []) and Li and Tsakiropoulos [] and references within and did not suffer from complete disintegration to powders, instead their scales spalled off and scale fragments disintegrated into powder. This suggests (i) that the simultaneous presence of Ge and Sn in the alloys “controlled and improved” the effect of Ge and (ii) that the synergy of these two elements with Hf, Ta, Ti, and W was also beneficial regarding control of pest oxidation. The oxidation resistance of the alloy JZ2 at 800 °C was slightly improved, most likely because of its lower vol.% of the Nbss and higher Sn+Ge content, compared with the alloy JZ1. The results of this work and the literature suggest that additional research should aim to find out whether the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys with Ta and W additions in the pest regime could be improved with simultaneous addition of Sn and Ge with Al and Cr.

In this work, the RM(Nb)IC alloy Nb–30Ti–10Si–5Cr–5Sn–3Fe–2Al–2Hf (NV2) was studied in the as-cast and heat-treated conditions; its isothermal oxidation at 700, 800 and 900 °C and its room temperature hardness and specific strength were compared with other Sn-containing RM(Nb)ICs—in particular, the alloy Nb–24Ti–18Si–5Cr–5Fe–5Sn (NV5)—and with RCCAs and RHEAs. The addition of Fe (a) stabilised Nbss; A15–Nb3X (X = Al, Si and Sn) and Nb3Si; metastable Nb3Si-m’ and Nb5Si3 silicides; (b) supported the formation of eutectic Nbss + Nb5Si3; (c) suppressed pest oxidation at all three temperatures and (d) stabilised a Cr- and Fe-rich phase instead of a C14–Nb(Cr,Fe)2 Laves phase. Complex concentrated (or compositionally complex) and/or high entropy phases co-existed with “conventional” phases in all conditions and after oxidation at 800 °C. In NV2, the macrosegregation of Si decreased but liquation occurred at T >1200 °C. A solid solution free of Si and rich in Cr and Ti was stable after the heat treatments. In this work, alloy Nb–30Ti–10Si–5Cr–5Sn–3Fe–2Al–2Hf (NV2) was studied in the as-cast and heat-treated conditions: its isothermal oxidation at three pest oxidation temperatures and its room temperature hardness and specific strength were evaluated and compared with other Sn-containing RM(Nb)ICs—in particular, alloy NV5—and with RCCAs and RHEAs. The issues that motivated this research were resolved. The synergy of Fe with Al, Cr, Hf and Sn (a) stabilised Nbss; A15–Nb3X (X = Al, Si and Sn) and Nb3Si, metastable Nb3Si-m’ and Nb5Si3 silicides; (b) supported the formation of Nbss + Nb5Si3 eutectic in the cast microstructure; (c) suppressed pest oxidation in the temperature range 700–900 °C and (d) stabilised a Cr-rich π phase instead of a C14–Nb(Cr,Fe)2 Laves phase. Furthermore, it was shown that complex concentrated (CC) or high entropy (HE) phases coexisted with “conventional” phases in all conditions and after oxidation at 800 °C.

frame.system: A non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy system (e.g., compositionally complex alloys such as MgAlCuZnGd or AlMgₓTiSnZn) initially combining solid solutions with intermetallic compounds formed during rapid/induction melting, leading to a metastable microstructure with region-dependent phase distribution.
frame.goal: To mechanistically explain how the alloy’s non-equilibrium microstructure evolves over time or under thermal/corrosion environments and to correlate these structural changes with altered corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
frame.limitation: Previous studies mainly focused on hardness and room-temperature compression and did not resolve the transformation pathways from the as-cast or metastable states into evolved structural states that determine corrosion and oxidation performance. Additionally, the stable intermetallic compounds fostered by inherent constituent-property differences have not been linked clearly to these functional property changes.

decision.trend: Early work on lightweight, compositionally complex alloys – for instance, studies on induction‐melted Al–Mg‐rich alloys – first established that rapid melting yields a multiphase, metastable microstructure containing a mix of solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Later work on compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys and AlMgₓTiSnZn systems then correlated regional or Mg‐dependent phase stability with functional properties (mostly hardness and room‐temperature compression). In all cases, however, the transformation pathways from these as‐cast, metastable states to more stable configurations under environmental exposures (corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation) were left unresolved.
decision.unsolved: What remains unsolved is the mechanistic connection between the non‐equilibrium evolution—specifically, the transformation (e.g., coarsening or phase separation) of Mg‐rich metastable intermetallic components—and the resultant change in corrosion resistance and oxidation behavior. In other words, it is not yet clear how the selective transformation of Mg‐enriched phases alters the formation or stability of protective oxide scales during high‐temperature oxidation or shifts localized corrosion behavior.
decision.lever: Implement controlled thermal aging and environmental (oxidizing and corrosive) exposures on samples with identical initial metastable microstructures, while monitoring the evolution of Mg‐rich intermetallic phases (using, for example, in situ XRD or TEM).
decision.why: This experiment builds directly on the observed trend: prior studies have established that Mg content affects phase stability but did not trace how metastable microstructures transform under service conditions. By comparing a baseline as-cast alloy with heat‐treated counterparts under controlled oxidation/corrosion conditions, one can test the hypothesis that the selective transformation (e.g., coarsening or phase redistribution) of Mg‐rich intermetallics directly modifies the alloy’s corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation behavior. An outcome showing no change in phase evolution or corrosion/oxidation performance relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
